solar.title: SUNLIGHT ON MARS IS WEAKER
solar.text: Mars is about 1.5 times farther from the Sun than Earth. So sunlight there is a bit less than half as strong as on Earth.
solar.image: NASA photo of a sunset on Mars (Curiosity or Spirit)

solar.title: NO POWER AT NIGHT
solar.text: A day on Mars (a sol) lasts about 24 hours and 39 minutes. Solar panels only work while the Sun is up, so at night the base runs on batteries.
solar.image: NASA photo of a solar-powered lander's panels (InSight)

solar.title: A ROVER THAT KEPT GOING
solar.text: The solar-powered rover Opportunity was planned to work for 90 sols. It kept working for more than 5,000 sols, from 2004 to 2018!
solar.image: NASA image of the Opportunity rover

solar.title: A SOLAR HELICOPTER
solar.text: NASA's Ingenuity helicopter charged its batteries with a small solar panel. It was planned for 5 flights and flew 72 times on Mars.
solar.image: NASA photo of the Ingenuity helicopter on Mars

solar.title: DUST COVERS THE PANELS
solar.text: The InSight lander had two round solar panels, each about 2.2 meters wide. Dust slowly covered them, and its mission ended in December 2022 when power ran low.
solar.image: NASA selfie of InSight with dusty solar panels

solar.title: STORMS BLOCK THE SUN
solar.text: In 2018 a dust storm covered all of Mars. The sky got so dark that the rover Opportunity could not charge, and NASA lost contact with it.
solar.image: NASA before/after images of Mars in the 2018 global dust storm

solar.title: POWER WITHOUT THE SUN
solar.text: Curiosity and Perseverance don't use solar panels. A nuclear power source turns heat into about 110 watts of electricity, day and night.
solar.image: NASA photo of the Perseverance rover's power system (MMRTG)

battery.title: SAVING THE DAY FOR THE NIGHT
battery.text: Batteries store energy from the solar panels during the day. At night the whole base uses that stored energy.
battery.image: NASA diagram of a rover's power system

battery.title: COLD MARS NIGHTS
battery.text: Nights on Mars often fall below minus 70 degrees Celsius. Batteries must be kept warm, and heating them uses energy too.

battery.title: ROVER BATTERIES
battery.text: Perseverance carries two rechargeable lithium-ion batteries. They give extra power when the rover needs more than its power source makes.
battery.image: NASA image of the Perseverance rover

battery.title: EVERY WATT COUNTS
battery.text: Mission teams plan each sol around the energy they have. In our base, these are the things that use the battery (game numbers).

figure.title: OUR BASE: POWER USE PER SECOND

battery.image: NASA photo of the rover operations team planning a sol

battery.title: SLEEP MODE
battery.text: When power gets very low, a rover can switch almost everything off and wait. Opportunity did this during the 2018 dust storm.
battery.image: NASA image of Opportunity during the 2018 storm

battery.title: BATTERIES GET TIRED
battery.text: Rechargeable batteries hold a little less energy as they get older. Engineers check battery health so they don't run out by surprise.
battery.image: NASA photo of engineers testing rover batteries

battery.title: POWER FOR FUTURE BASES
battery.text: In 2018 NASA tested a small nuclear reactor called Kilopower. Reactors like it could power a base on the Moon or Mars, day and night.
battery.image: NASA photo of the Kilopower reactor test

life_support.title: WHAT IS MARS AIR?
life_support.text: Mars air is about 95% carbon dioxide and is very thin. People cannot breathe it, so the base must make its own oxygen.
life_support.image: NASA graphic of Mars atmosphere composition

life_support.title: MOXIE MADE OXYGEN
life_support.text: MOXIE, a machine on Perseverance, made oxygen from Mars air. From 2021 to 2023 it made 122 grams, up to 12 grams per hour.
life_support.image: NASA photo of MOXIE being put into Perseverance

life_support.title: HOW MUCH AIR DO WE NEED?
life_support.text: One astronaut uses about 0.84 kg of oxygen every day. That is much more than MOXIE made in its whole mission!
life_support.image: NASA photo of the space station's oxygen system

life_support.title: CLEANING OUT CO2
life_support.text: We breathe out carbon dioxide, and too much makes people sleepy and gives headaches. Life support machines pull CO2 out of the air.
life_support.image: NASA photo of the space station's CO2 removal system

life_support.title: RECYCLING WATER
life_support.text: The space station recycles about 98% of its water, even from sweat and urine. A Mars base would have to recycle almost everything too.

figure.title: WATER RECYCLED ON THE SPACE STATION

life_support.image: NASA photo of the space station water recovery system

life_support.title: PLANTS HELP BREATHE
life_support.text: Plants take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen. Future bases may use greenhouses as part of their life support.
life_support.image: NASA photo of plants growing on the space station

greenhouse.title: SALAD IN SPACE
greenhouse.text: In 2015 astronauts on the space station ate red romaine lettuce they grew themselves. The plant chamber is called Veggie.
greenhouse.image: NASA photo of astronauts eating space-grown lettuce

greenhouse.title: LIGHTS FOR PLANTS
greenhouse.text: Space greenhouses use LED lights, mostly red and blue, instead of sunlight. Lights use power, just like our Crop Lamp.
greenhouse.image: NASA photo of the Veggie chamber's pink-purple light

greenhouse.title: SALTY MARS SOIL
greenhouse.text: In 2008 the Phoenix lander found perchlorate in Mars soil, about half a percent. It is bad for people and plants, so soil must be cleaned first.
greenhouse.image: NASA photo of Phoenix lander's scoop and soil

greenhouse.title: HOT PEPPERS IN ORBIT
greenhouse.text: In 2021 astronauts grew chile peppers on the space station. Peppers took about four months to grow.
greenhouse.image: NASA photo of chile peppers growing on the space station

greenhouse.title: WATER FROM ICE
greenhouse.text: Mars has water ice at its poles and under the ground. In 2008 the Phoenix lander dug up ice just under the soil.
greenhouse.image: NASA Phoenix images of ice in a trench

greenhouse.title: FOOD FOR A LONG TRIP
greenhouse.text: A trip to Mars and back could take years. Growing some food on Mars would mean carrying less from Earth.
greenhouse.image: NASA concept art of a Mars greenhouse

shelter.title: WHAT IS SHIELDING?
shelter.text: Shielding means putting material between people and radiation. Materials full of hydrogen, like water and plastic, block particles well.

shelter.title: RADIATION EVERY DAY
shelter.text: Curiosity measures about 210 microgray of radiation on a normal day on Mars. On 2024-05-20 a solar storm gave 8,100 in one go!
shelter.image: NASA image of Curiosity's RAD instrument

shelter.title: HIDING UNDER MARS SOIL
shelter.text: A thick layer of Mars soil or rock above a base would block most particles. Caves or buried rooms could make good shelters.
shelter.image: NASA concept art of a Mars base covered with soil

shelter.title: A SHELTER MADE OF BAGS
shelter.text: In NASA's Orion spaceship, astronauts can build a storm shelter from their supply bags. More stuff around you means more shielding.
shelter.image: NASA photo of the Orion radiation shelter test

shelter.title: NO MAGNETIC SHIELD
shelter.text: Earth's magnetic field and thick air protect us from solar particles. Mars lost its global magnetic field long ago, so its ground gets much more radiation.
shelter.image: NASA MAVEN graphic of the solar wind hitting Mars

suit_bay.title: A SPACESUIT IS A TINY SPACESHIP
suit_bay.text: A spacesuit gives air to breathe, keeps the right pressure, and keeps the astronaut warm or cool. Outside, it is all that keeps them alive.
suit_bay.image: NASA photo of an astronaut in a spacesuit

suit_bay.title: TESTING SUITS ON MARS
suit_bay.text: Perseverance carries five small samples of spacesuit material. Scientists watch how Mars sunlight and dust change them.
suit_bay.image: NASA image of the SHERLOC calibration target with suit samples

suit_bay.title: STICKY, SHARP DUST
suit_bay.text: Moon dust stuck to Apollo astronauts' suits and wore them down. Mars dust is also fine and sticky, so suits must be cleaned.
suit_bay.image: NASA photo of a dusty Apollo spacesuit

suit_bay.title: HOW LONG IS A SPACEWALK?
suit_bay.text: Spacewalks outside the space station usually last about 6 and a half hours. On Mars, crews must get back fast when danger comes.
suit_bay.image: NASA photo of a spacewalk outside the space station

comms_dish.title: MESSAGES TAKE MINUTES
comms_dish.text: Radio waves travel at the speed of light, but Mars is far away. A message takes between about 3 and 22 minutes to arrive, depending on where the planets are.
comms_dish.image: NASA graphic of Earth and Mars orbits

comms_dish.title: GIANT EARS ON EARTH
comms_dish.text: NASA's Deep Space Network has three big antenna sites: California, Spain and Australia. As Earth spins, one of them can always hear Mars.
comms_dish.image: NASA photo of a Deep Space Network antenna

comms_dish.title: ORBITERS PASS IT ON
comms_dish.text: Rovers send most of their data to spacecraft circling Mars, like the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter. The orbiters send it on to Earth.
comms_dish.image: NASA image of the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter

comms_dish.title: WHEN THE SUN IS IN THE WAY
comms_dish.text: About every two years the Sun sits between Earth and Mars. Mission teams stop sending commands for about two weeks until it moves.
comms_dish.image: NASA graphic of Mars solar conjunction
